name: Serverless Architectures
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in Serverless Architectures as a competency should be able to design, implement, and operate solutions using major cloud provider serverless platforms (AWS Lambda, API Gateway, EventBridge, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, Step Functions, S3, CloudWatch; Azure Functions, Event Grid, Service Bus, Cosmos DB; GCP Cloud Functions/Run, Pub/Sub, Firestore), model event-driven and integration patterns (event notification, event-carried state, queues, streams, schema management, idempotency, retries, DLQs), build and secure APIs with managed gateways (REST, HTTP, WebSocket, CORS, JWT/OAuth2, custom authorizers, Cognito/Azure AD), handle data persistence using NoSQL, serverless relational, object storage, and caching, and manage scalability, concurrency, and performance (cold starts, memory/time tuning, batching, streaming, load testing). They should address reliability and distributed systems concerns (retries, backoff, circuit breakers, compensating actions, health checks, multi-AZ resilience), apply security best practices (least-privilege IAM, secret management, network controls, encryption, compliance logging), optimize for cost (invocation, memory, storage, monitoring costs, anti-patterns, cost explorer tools), implement observability (structured logging, custom metrics, tracing, dashboards, alarms), write and run tests (unit, integration, local emulation, cloud logs/traces), define infrastructure-as-code (SAM, Serverless Framework, CDK, Terraform, Bicep/ARM, GCP DM), automate CI/CD (build, test, deploy, blue/green/canary, secure config, static analysis), support operational readiness (SLOs, runbooks, incident response, dependency upgrades, tagging), and collaborate through documentation, design reviews, integration with legacy systems, shared patterns, and mentoring.

{"sections":[{"name":"Core Serverless Fundamentals & Mental Models","scope_included":"- Understand the definition and scope of serverless architectures: managed compute, managed scaling, pay-per-use, and heavy reliance on managed services (FaaS + BaaS)
- Distinguish clearly between serverless, containers, PaaS, and traditional IaaS; know when serverless is appropriate vs when it is not
- Apply event-driven thinking: model systems around events, triggers, and reactions rather than long-lived servers
- Understand key building blocks: Functions-as-a-Service (FaaS), managed APIs, event buses, queues, streams, schedulers, managed databases, object storage, and workflow/orchestration services
- Reason about the shared-responsibility model in serverless: what the cloud provider manages vs what the team must handle
- Understand cold starts, warm starts, and lifecycle of serverless compute instances; recognize their impact on latency and cost
- Recognize typical serverless use cases: APIs, data processing, integration, scheduled jobs, lightweight workflows, backends for mobile/web/IoT
- Understand basic multi-tenancy implications of serverless platforms and how isolation works (at least conceptually)
- Understand limitations/quotas of serverless platforms (concurrency limits, timeouts, payload sizes, deployment size, etc.) and how they influence architecture and design
- Articulate trade-offs between simplicity and flexibility when heavily relying on managed serverless services (lock-in, observability, limited customization)
- Apply core cloud-native principles to serverless: statelessness, immutability, horizontal scaling, design for failure, infrastructure-as-code mindset","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Cloud Provider Serverless Platforms & Core Services","scope_included":"- Work comfortably with at least one major cloud provider’s serverless stack (e.g., AWS is typical, but Azure/GCP equivalently acceptable)
- For AWS-centric experience:
  - Design and implement solutions with AWS Lambda, API Gateway (REST/HTTP/WebSocket), EventBridge, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, Step Functions, S3, CloudWatch
  - Understand basic configuration options of Lambda: memory, timeout, environment variables, concurrency, layers, execution roles
- For Azure-centric experience:
  - Use Azure Functions with major trigger/binding types (HTTP, Timer, Queue, Service Bus, Blob, Event Grid)
  - Apply Azure API Management, Event Grid, Service Bus, Cosmos DB, Storage Queues/Blobs in serverless solutions
- For GCP-centric experience:
  - Use Cloud Functions/Cloud Run for serverless compute and integrate with Pub/Sub, Cloud Scheduler, Cloud Storage, Firestore/Datastore
  - Understand differences between Cloud Functions and Cloud Run in terms of scaling, isolation and capabilities
- Understand and use managed workflow/orchestration (e.g., AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, GCP Workflows) for multi-step business processes
- Understand role of identity and access services (e.g., IAM, Azure AD, Cloud IAM) in controlling access to serverless components
- Be able to select appropriate managed services (queue vs topic vs event bus vs stream; NoSQL vs relational vs object storage) for common scenarios in a serverless context
- Understand regional aspects and high-level multi-AZ resilience characteristics of managed serverless services on the chosen cloud","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Event-Driven & Integration Patterns","scope_included":"- Model end-to-end flows using common event-driven patterns (event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing at a conceptual level)
- Design event producers, consumers, and event routers/buses; define event contracts (schemas, versioning, evolution)
- Use messaging services (queues, topics, streams) effectively for decoupling services and implementing asynchronous workflows
- Understand and apply at-least-once and at-most-once delivery semantics, including idempotency strategies in serverless handlers
- Design serverless consumers that handle retries, dead-letter queues, and poison message handling
- Know when to use direct synchronous invocation (e.g., HTTP) vs asynchronous event triggers for different business needs
- Integrate serverless functions with external services (SaaS, on-prem systems, partner APIs) via webhooks, polling, or integration services (e.g., API Gateway integrations, Logic Apps, EventBridge, Azure Event Grid)
- Handle backpressure and bursty traffic using queues/streams and concurrency controls in serverless environments
- Understand schema management approaches for events (e.g., JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf conceptually) and how to evolve events without breaking consumers
- Design for eventual consistency and asynchronous processing where appropriate in serverless systems","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"API & Edge Design with Serverless","scope_included":"- Design and implement RESTful/HTTP APIs backed by serverless functions, using managed API gateways
- Define resource modeling, routes, methods, and status codes appropriate for typical CRUD and workflow APIs
- Use API gateway features: request/response mapping, validation, throttling, rate limiting, API keys, usage plans, CORS configuration
- Understand basic API authentication and authorization patterns in serverless: JWT/OAuth2, Cognito/B2C/Identity Platform integration, custom authorizers/handlers
- Design for versioning and lifecycle management of APIs (e.g., v1/v2, stage-based promotion)
- Understand edge/serverless at the edge (e.g., Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions, Cloudflare Workers, Azure Front Door Rules) at a conceptual level and use it for simple use cases (header manipulation, redirects, basic caching logic)
- Integrate serverless APIs with frontend clients (SPAs, mobile apps) including handling CORS, latency concerns, pagination, and response shaping
- Apply patterns for file upload and download via signed URLs to offload data transfer from functions to storage/CDN
- Recognize when GraphQL, gRPC, or API aggregation patterns may be beneficial and how serverless can back them (high-level understanding, basic implementation ability)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Data Management & Persistence in Serverless Systems","scope_included":"- Design data access patterns suitable for stateless functions (short-lived connections, connection pooling patterns for relational DBs, use of proxies/pools if needed)
- Understand strengths and limitations of NoSQL datastores (e.g., DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Firestore) in a serverless context: partitioning, throughput, consistency, query limits
- Model data for common serverless use cases: key-value patterns, document stores, time-series, event logs
- Use serverless-friendly relational offerings where appropriate (e.g., Aurora Serverless, Azure SQL with serverless tiers, Cloud SQL with autoscaling concepts)
- Understand and manage transaction boundaries in a distributed serverless architecture: when to use eventual consistency vs explicit transactions
- Implement basic patterns for distributed data consistency (sagas via workflows, compensating transactions, idempotent updates)
- Use object storage (e.g., S3, Blob Storage, GCS) with appropriate organization (prefixing, folder conventions) and metadata practices
- Apply data lifecycle and retention strategies using storage tiering, TTL, and archival for logs and business data
- Understand constraints and best practices for handling large payloads, buffering, and streaming in and out of serverless functions
- Be aware of limits of in-memory state and use of external state stores (caches, databases, durable entities) instead of relying on local memory or disk
- Design basic caching strategies in a serverless environment (edge caching via CDN, application-level cache, database query caching)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Scalability, Performance & Concurrency Management","scope_included":"- Explain how serverless platforms scale instances based on events/requests, including per-region and per-function concurrency concepts
- Configure function memory/CPU and timeout settings appropriately based on workload characteristics and performance requirements
- Understand cold start factors (language, VPC attachment, package size, initialization code) and apply patterns to mitigate them within reason
- Design for handling traffic spikes: use queues/streams, throttling, and backoff strategies to protect downstream systems
- Evaluate and tune concurrency limits at function and account/subscription level to balance throughput, cost, and downstream safety
- Understand typical performance characteristics of supported runtimes (Node.js, Python, Java, .NET, etc.) in serverless environments and select runtimes sensibly
- Profile and optimize hot paths in serverless functions: reduce external calls, optimize data serialization, batch operations where appropriate
- Implement streaming/batch processing with serverless (e.g., Kinesis/Event Hubs/PubSub triggers) and tune batch sizes, parallelism, checkpointing
- Recognize when serverless may not meet latency/throughput needs and when to combine it with containers/other compute options
- Apply simple load and performance testing approaches for serverless APIs and event consumers to validate scaling behavior","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Reliability, Resilience & Distributed Systems Concerns","scope_included":"- Design serverless workflows that tolerate transient failures using retries, backoff, and circuit-breaker-like behavior (where supported)
- Configure and interpret built-in retry policies for triggers (queues, streams, event buses, HTTP) and understand their impact on downstream systems
- Use dead-letter queues, parking lots, or error topics to capture and handle failed events/messages
- Understand partial failures in distributed workflows and apply compensating actions (often via orchestrators like Step Functions/Durable Functions/Workflows)
- Design idempotent operations to safely handle replays and duplicates
- Implement simple health checks and basic synthetic monitoring paths for critical serverless endpoints
- Consider multi-AZ and regional characteristics of managed services when designing for availability; understand default redundancy guarantees
- Plan for graceful degradation of non-critical features during downstream outages (e.g., fallback responses, queuing behavior)
- Understand timeouts across layers (client, API gateway, function, downstream services) and coordinate them to avoid cascading failures
- Use workflow/orchestration services to increase reliability of long-running or multi-step processes instead of manually building state machines inside functions","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Security, Identity & Compliance in Serverless","scope_included":"- Apply least-privilege IAM principles to functions and serverless resources (fine-grained roles, managed identities, service principals)
- Configure authentication and authorization for serverless APIs using built-in identity services (e.g., Cognito, Azure AD, Firebase Auth) or external IdPs
- Understand key security responsibilities in serverless: secret management, input validation, output encoding, dependency management, runtime patching (where applicable)
- Use managed secret stores (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and avoid hardcoding secrets
- Handle common web/API vulnerabilities (OWASP API Top 10) in serverless code: injection, broken auth, insecure direct object references, etc.
- Manage network-level security controls (VPC/subnet integration, private endpoints, service endpoints, firewall rules) for functions that access private resources
- Understand implications of public vs private endpoints in API Gateways and event sources
- Ensure data-in-transit encryption (TLS) and be aware of data-at-rest encryption defaults/options in managed services
- Address basic compliance concerns (logging access, audit trails, retention) and understand how serverless logs and events can support audits
- Apply secure deployment practices (signing artifacts where applicable, restricting who can deploy/modify serverless resources)
- Recognize and avoid insecure patterns like long-lived tokens in code, over-privileged roles, or unrestricted public triggers","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Cost Modeling, Optimization & Governance in Serverless","scope_included":"- Understand the main cost drivers of serverless workloads: invocations, execution time, memory size, data transfer, managed service usage
- Estimate and compare costs for common architectures (API-based, queue-based, streaming pipelines) at a rough order-of-magnitude level
- Use provider tools (e.g., AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, GCP Billing) to observe serverless-related costs and identify high-cost components
- Optimize function configuration (memory/time) to balance performance and cost; understand that more memory can sometimes reduce total cost by reducing duration
- Design patterns that reduce unnecessary invocations (e.g., using native integrations, aggregation/batching, push vs poll)
- Apply basic data lifecycle and storage tiering to manage storage costs for logs, events, and application data
- Recognize anti-patterns that increase cost (chatty functions, overly granular functions, excessive synchronous chains, large responses via API) and refactor them
- Understand account/subscription/project-level guardrails (budgets, alerts, quotas) for serverless usage and participate in their configuration with cloud/platform teams
- Consider multi-environment cost implications (dev/test/stage/prod) and adopt approaches like smaller quotas or shorter retention in non-prod environments
- Communicate cost implications of design choices to stakeholders and factor cost into architectural decisions at an intermediate level","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Observability: Logging, Metrics & Tracing for Serverless","scope_included":"- Implement structured, contextual logging within serverless functions (correlation IDs, request IDs, key business identifiers)
- Use cloud-native logging services (e.g., CloudWatch Logs, Azure Monitor, Stackdriver Logging) to query, filter, and analyze logs
- Define and publish custom metrics (e.g., errors, latency, throughput, business KPIs) from serverless code where needed
- Understand and use platform metrics (invocations, duration, errors, throttles, concurrent executions, DLQ counts) to monitor health and performance
- Configure alarms/alerts based on metrics (e.g., error rate, latency, DLQ length, throttling) using cloud monitoring services
- Understand basics of distributed tracing in a serverless environment and integrate tracing SDKs (e.g., AWS X-Ray, Azure Application Insights, OpenTelemetry)
- Trace end-to-end flows across multiple functions and managed services to troubleshoot latency or failure points
- Implement log correlation across services using trace IDs, spans, and correlation headers
- Create dashboards or views that provide a coherent picture of a serverless application’s health for engineering and operations teams
- Use observability data to drive iterative improvement of reliability, performance, and cost posture","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Testing, Debugging & Local Development for Serverless","scope_included":"- Write unit tests for serverless handlers with appropriate mocking of cloud SDKs and external dependencies
- Implement integration tests that exercise functions against real or emulated cloud services (e.g., local emulators, test stacks, sandboxes)
- Use local development tools/emulators where available (e.g., SAM CLI, LocalStack, Azure Functions Core Tools, Firebase emulators, GCP emulators) for rapid feedback
- Set up test data and fixtures for common serverless event sources (API events, queue messages, stream records, scheduled events, storage events)
- Debug functions locally using breakpoints and local runtimes for supported languages, and know when cloud-only debugging/logging is required
- Interpret cloud logs, metrics, and traces to diagnose and fix common production issues (timeouts, memory errors, permission errors, throttling)
- Use canary testing or limited-rollout mechanisms (e.g., $LATEST vs versions/aliases, deployment slots) in collaboration with CI/CD
- Adopt patterns that make serverless code testable (separation of pure logic from handler glue code, dependency injection, configuration isolation)
- Participate in defining and maintaining test environments and test datasets specific to serverless workflows
- Understand limitations of local testing for fully managed services and know how to mitigate them with targeted in-cloud tests","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Infrastructure-as-Code & Automation for Serverless","scope_included":"- Define serverless resources using infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tools (e.g., AWS SAM, Serverless Framework, AWS CDK, Terraform, Azure Bicep/ARM, GCP Deployment Manager)
- Model functions, API gateways, event sources, queues, topics, databases, and IAM roles/policies declaratively
- Use IaC modules/stacks to organize serverless infrastructure into manageable units (per-service, per-domain, per-environment)
- Parameterize IaC templates for different environments (dev/test/stage/prod) with appropriate configuration management
- Understand how IaC changes map to actual cloud resources (create/update/replace behaviors) and avoid destructive changes accidentally
- Validate and lint IaC templates using available tooling (e.g., cfn-lint, tflint, checkov, cdk-nag) as part of development workflow
- Use automation scripts/commands to deploy, update, and roll back serverless stacks reliably
- Store IaC source in version control and participate in code review processes for infrastructure changes
- Understand and apply basic drift detection concepts (ensuring actual infrastructure matches IaC definitions)
- Collaborate with platform or DevOps teams to align serverless IaC with broader cloud governance patterns (naming, tagging, network standards)","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"CI/CD & Release Engineering for Serverless","scope_included":"- Design and maintain basic CI/CD pipelines for serverless applications using common tools (e.g., GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild, Jenkins)
- Automate build, test, package, and deployment of serverless code and IaC templates
- Use environment-specific configurations and secrets within pipelines securely (vaults, key management, environment variables)
- Implement safe deployment strategies for serverless: versioning, aliases, blue/green or canary rollouts where supported by the platform
- Integrate static code analysis, security scanning, and IaC validation into the CI pipeline for serverless repositories
- Set up automated tests (unit + selected integration tests) as gating checks in CI before deployment
- Use pipeline logs and deployment history to troubleshoot deployment failures and rollbacks
- Coordinate pipeline design with branching strategies (trunk-based, GitFlow variants) used by the team
- Ensure CI/CD pipelines produce and maintain artifacts (packages, templates, changelogs) necessary for audit and traceability
- Collaborate with SRE/Platform teams to align serverless release practices with organization-wide release and change-management processes","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Operational Readiness, Runbooks & Production Management","scope_included":"- Participate in defining SLOs/SLIs for key serverless services (availability, latency, error rate) and map them to monitoring/alerting
- Contribute to and follow operational runbooks for common incidents in serverless systems (e.g., elevated error rates, DLQ spikes, throttling, cost anomalies)
- Perform routine operational tasks: updating environment variables, rotating secrets, adjusting limits/quotas in coordination with platform admins
- Use observability and logging tools during incidents to quickly identify impact, root cause candidates, and potential mitigations
- Understand basic incident response workflows and roles (on-call, incident commander, comms) when serverless components are involved
- Support maintenance tasks such as dependency upgrades, runtime version changes, and deprecations of older APIs or services
- Track and respond to provider deprecation notices or breaking changes that affect serverless components (in collaboration with senior staff)
- Evaluate and implement small operational improvements (e.g., new alerts, dashboard tweaks, better DLQ handling) based on incident/postmortem learnings
- Apply tagging/labeling standards on serverless resources to support operations, cost allocation, and ownership clarity
- Consider capacity and limit management (concurrency limits, throughput settings, quotas) as an ongoing operational concern, not a one-time setup","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Design Documentation & Cross-Team Work","scope_included":"- Produce clear, concise design documentation for serverless components: context diagrams, sequence diagrams, event flows, API specs
- Document event schemas, contracts, and expectations (e.g., validation rules, retry semantics, error formats) for downstream and upstream teams
- Participate actively in architecture/design reviews, providing input on serverless-related trade-offs and risks
- Communicate with non-serverless or legacy system teams to design integrations, clarify responsibilities, and negotiate interfaces
- Keep runbooks, onboarding docs, and READMEs for serverless services up to date, including deployment instructions, environment details, and troubleshooting tips
- Mentor junior engineers on serverless fundamentals, best practices, and common pitfalls, using code reviews and pair programming
- Collaborate with security, compliance, and platform teams to ensure serverless solutions meet organizational standards
- Use ticketing and documentation systems (e.g., Jira/Azure Boards + Confluence/Wikis) to track work and maintain traceability of serverless changes
- Contribute to shared libraries/templates/blueprints that standardize serverless patterns across teams (logging, auth, error handling)
- Participate in post-incident reviews involving serverless systems, documenting learnings and helping to define action items","is_non_core_section":true}]}
